title: State and Command
scopeHtml: Scope: State machines and Command with undo/redo, refactors, Java and Kotlin, real examples. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: State: the idea
notes.html:
The State pattern lets an object change its behaviour when its internal state changes, by delegating to a separate object per state. Instead of if (state == X) in every method, each state is a class that knows what each action means in that state.

Use it when an object has a handful of modes and the same method behaves differently per mode: vending machine, order lifecycle, media player, TCP connection, document (draft, review, published).

Before (flag + if chain in every method):

class Player {
    enum S { STOPPED, PLAYING, PAUSED }
    S s = S.STOPPED;
    void pressPlay() {
        if (s == S.STOPPED) { start(); s = S.PLAYING; }
        else if (s == S.PLAYING) { pause(); s = S.PAUSED; }
        else if (s == S.PAUSED) { resume(); s = S.PLAYING; }
    }
    void pressStop() { if (s != S.STOPPED) { halt(); s = S.STOPPED; } }
}

With 3 states and 5 actions you can have up to 15 branches spread over methods. Add a "Buffering" state and you edit every method.

After:

interface PlayerState {
    void play(Player p); void stop(Player p);
}
class Stopped implements PlayerState {
    public void play(Player p) { p.startAudio(); p.setState(new Playing()); }
    public void stop(Player p) { /* already stopped: ignore */ }
}
class Playing implements PlayerState {
    public void play(Player p) { p.pauseAudio(); p.setState(new Paused()); }
    public void stop(Player p) { p.haltAudio(); p.setState(new Stopped()); }
}
class Paused implements PlayerState {
    public void play(Player p) { p.resumeAudio(); p.setState(new Playing()); }
    public void stop(Player p) { p.haltAudio(); p.setState(new Stopped()); }
}
class Player {
    private PlayerState state = new Stopped();
    void setState(PlayerState s) { state = s; }
    void pressPlay() { state.play(this); }
    void pressStop() { state.stop(this); }
}
+------------+  state   +-----------------+
| Player     |--------->| <<interface>>   |
| + pressPlay|          | PlayerState     |
| + pressStop|          | play(), stop()  |
+------------+          +--------+--------+
                                 ^
                    +------------+-----------+
                 Stopped      Playing       Paused

Kotlin variant (sealed class, compiler checks every state is handled):

sealed interface PlayerState {
    object Stopped : PlayerState
    object Playing : PlayerState
    object Paused : PlayerState
}
class Player {
    var state: PlayerState = PlayerState.Stopped; private set
    fun onPlay() { state = when (state) {
        PlayerState.Stopped -> PlayerState.Playing
        PlayerState.Playing -> PlayerState.Paused
        PlayerState.Paused  -> PlayerState.Playing
    } }
}

Two valid styles: state-as-object (behaviour inside state classes) and state-as-data with a when (transitions in one function). Kotlin favours the second for small machines.

Decision gravity. Choosing State is a moderate refactor, reversible. The one-way door is persisting states: once "PAID", "SHIPPED" are stored in a DB column, renaming or splitting states needs a data migration.

Everyday analogy. A traffic light: pressing the pedestrian button means something different on red, green and amber.

Common interview traps.

  • Not drawing the transition table. Say states, events, and what is illegal.
  • Allocating a new state object on each transition; stateless states can be singletons (Kotlin object).
  • Letting every state touch every field; the context should expose a small API.

notes.title: Finite state machines in practice
notes.html:
A finite state machine (FSM) is a set of states, a set of events, and a transition table: (current state, event) -> (next state, action). It makes illegal transitions impossible by construction, which is the real value.

Order state machine
                 pay            ship            deliver
   CREATED ------------> PAID ----------> SHIPPED --------> DELIVERED
      |                    |                  |
      | cancel             | refund           | (no cancel here)
      v                    v
  CANCELLED            REFUNDED

Worked example (table-driven). 5 states x 4 events = 20 cells. Only 6 are legal. A table makes that explicit:

enum OrderState { CREATED, PAID, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, CANCELLED, REFUNDED }
enum Event { PAY, SHIP, DELIVER, CANCEL, REFUND }

class OrderFsm {
    private static final Map<OrderState, Map<Event, OrderState>> T = Map.of(
        OrderState.CREATED, Map.of(Event.PAY, OrderState.PAID, Event.CANCEL, OrderState.CANCELLED),
        OrderState.PAID,    Map.of(Event.SHIP, OrderState.SHIPPED, Event.REFUND, OrderState.REFUNDED),
        OrderState.SHIPPED, Map.of(Event.DELIVER, OrderState.DELIVERED));
    OrderState next(OrderState s, Event e) {
        OrderState n = T.getOrDefault(s, Map.of()).get(e);
        if (n == null) throw new IllegalStateException(s + " + " + e);
        return n;
    }
}
val table = mapOf(
    (Created to Pay) to Paid, (Created to Cancel) to Cancelled,
    (Paid to Ship) to Shipped, (Paid to Refund) to Refunded,
    (Shipped to Deliver) to Delivered)
fun next(s: OrderState, e: Event) = table[s to e] ?: error("illegal $s + $e")

Real FSMs. Android: Activity lifecycle, MediaPlayer states (Idle, Initialized, Prepared, Started, Paused, Stopped, End; calling start() in the wrong state throws IllegalStateException), WorkManager.State (ENQUEUED, RUNNING, SUCCEEDED, FAILED, CANCELLED, BLOCKED). Backend: TCP (LISTEN, SYN_RECEIVED, ESTABLISHED, FIN_WAIT, TIME_WAIT ...), Stripe PaymentIntent statuses, AWS Step Functions, Kubernetes pod phases. Libraries: Spring Statemachine, Android StateMachine (internal), Kotlin libs such as Tinder StateMachine.

Production incident pattern. Two concurrent requests both read an order in PAID and both ship it, double-shipping. Symptom: duplicate shipment IDs, state log shows two PAID -> SHIPPED rows. Fix: do the transition atomically, UPDATE orders SET state='SHIPPED' WHERE id=? AND state='PAID' and check affected rows = 1 (optimistic guard), or use a version column.

Decision gravity. A transition table is cheap to write and expensive to change once other services depend on the state names. Add states rarely; prefer adding a sub-state or a flag over splitting a published state.

Everyday analogy. A board game: each square allows only certain moves; the rulebook is the transition table.

Common interview traps.

  • Concurrency: reading state then writing without a guard.
  • Forgetting a terminal state and an error/timeout transition.
  • Letting any code set the state field directly; funnel everything through next.

notes.title: When NOT to use State
notes.html:
• Two states (on/off): a boolean is enough.
  • State affects one method only: a when in that method is simpler than classes.
  • States differ in data, not behaviour: use an enum with fields.
  • Transitions are driven by a huge external workflow (approvals across weeks, multiple actors): use a workflow engine (Temporal, Camunda, Step Functions) instead of hand-rolled classes.

State vs Strategy (the classic confusion): structure is nearly identical (context + interface + implementations). Strategy: the client chooses the algorithm and it rarely changes by itself. State: the object itself swaps its state object when events occur, and states know about each other (Stopped creates Playing).

Cost. One class per state in Java (5 states = 5 files plus interface). Transitions are scattered across classes, so one cannot see the whole graph in one place; a table or a diagram in docs fixes that.

Everyday analogy. A strategy is choosing a route; a state is the car being in gear 1, 2 or reverse (the same pedal does different things).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "State = Strategy". Explain who triggers the change.
  • Using State when a simple enum + when is more readable.

notes.title: Command: the idea
notes.html:
Command turns a request into an object. Instead of calling light.on() directly, you create TurnOnCommand(light) that carries what to do, on what, with what arguments. Because it is an object you can queue it, log it, schedule it, send it over a network, and undo it.

Roles: Command (interface with execute()), Receiver (does the real work), Invoker (button, queue, scheduler), Client (wires them).

+---------+ executes +-------------+ calls +-----------+
| Invoker |--------->| <<interface>>|------>| Receiver  |
| (button)|          | Command      |       | (Light)   |
+---------+          | execute()    |       +-----------+
                     | undo()       |
                     +------+-------+
                            ^
                 +----------+----------+
            TurnOnCmd          TurnOffCmd

Before: a remote with hard-coded buttons.

class Remote {
    Light light; Fan fan;
    void button1() { light.on(); }
    void button2() { fan.start(); }   // rewiring needs code changes
}

After:

interface Command { void execute(); void undo(); }

class LightOn implements Command {
    private final Light light;
    LightOn(Light l) { light = l; }
    public void execute() { light.on(); }
    public void undo()    { light.off(); }
}
class Remote {
    private Command[] slots = new Command[5];
    void set(int i, Command c) { slots[i] = c; }
    void press(int i) { slots[i].execute(); }
}

Kotlin variant. Without undo, a command is just () -> Unit:

val queue = ArrayDeque<() -> Unit>()
queue += { light.on() }
queue += { fan.start() }
while (queue.isNotEmpty()) queue.removeFirst()()

Real examples. Runnable and Callable (a command with no undo), ExecutorService.submit; Android Handler.post(Runnable), WorkManager Worker (persisted command with retries), Intent + PendingIntent (a command handed to another process to run later); database transaction logs and write-ahead logs (commands replayed on recovery); Redux/MVI actions; job queues like Sidekiq/Celery tasks; Kafka messages used as commands.

Decision gravity. Making requests objects is a modest cost and a flexible door. The one-way part is serialising commands (persisted queues, event sourcing): old command shapes must stay readable forever.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant order slip: the waiter writes it down; the kitchen cooks later, in order; the slip can be cancelled or reprinted.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing Command with Strategy: Command packages a request (what to do, to whom, with what); Strategy packages an algorithm.
  • Forgetting commands may fail; queued commands need retry/idempotency.
  • Executing a command twice by accident (non-idempotent commands in a retry queue).

notes.title: Undo and redo with Command
notes.html:
Undo works by storing, for each command, enough information to reverse it, and keeping a history stack. Two stacks: undoStack and redoStack.

Algorithm:

  1. execute(cmd): run it, push to undoStack, clear redoStack.
  2. undo(): pop from undoStack, call cmd.undo(), push to redoStack.
  3. redo(): pop from redoStack, call cmd.execute(), push to undoStack.

Worked example (text editor). Document "Hello". Type " World" (cmd1: insert at 5, text " World"), then delete 3 chars (cmd2: delete range 8..11, saved text "rld"). Stack: [cmd1, cmd2]. Undo pops cmd2 and re-inserts "rld" -> "Hello World". Undo again pops cmd1 and deletes " World" -> "Hello". Redo re-applies cmd1. Memory: storing deltas (a few bytes each) rather than a full copy of the document: 10,000 edits x about 50 bytes = 500 KB, versus 10,000 x 100 KB = 1 GB if you snapshot each time.

class History {
    private final Deque<Command> undo = new ArrayDeque<>(), redo = new ArrayDeque<>();
    void run(Command c) { c.execute(); undo.push(c); redo.clear(); }
    void undo() { if (!undo.isEmpty()) { Command c = undo.pop(); c.undo(); redo.push(c); } }
    void redo() { if (!redo.isEmpty()) { Command c = redo.pop(); c.execute(); undo.push(c); } }
}

class InsertText implements Command {
    private final StringBuilder doc; private final int pos; private final String text;
    InsertText(StringBuilder d, int p, String t) { doc = d; pos = p; text = t; }
    public void execute() { doc.insert(pos, text); }
    public void undo()    { doc.delete(pos, pos + text.length()); }
}
class History {
    private val undo = ArrayDeque<Command>(); private val redo = ArrayDeque<Command>()
    fun run(c: Command) { c.execute(); undo.addLast(c); redo.clear() }
    fun undo() { undo.removeLastOrNull()?.also { it.undo(); redo.addLast(it) } }
    fun redo() { redo.removeLastOrNull()?.also { it.execute(); undo.addLast(it) } }
}

Two strategies for undo.

  • Inverse command (above): small, fast, but each command needs a correct inverse. Not every action is reversible (send email, charge card).
  • Memento / snapshot (next notes): store prior state; simple but memory-heavy. Photoshop-style apps use a hybrid (deltas plus periodic snapshots).

Extras for seniors. Macro command = composite of commands (undo reverses in reverse order). Merge consecutive keystrokes into one command so Ctrl+Z undoes a word, not a letter. Cap the stack (for example 100 entries) to bound memory. In collaborative editors (Google Docs), undo must be per-user and transformed against others' edits (Operational Transform or CRDTs).

When NOT to use Command.

  • A single direct method call with no queue, log or undo: just call it.
  • Side effects that cannot be reversed: model compensating actions (refund) instead of pretending to undo.
  • Very hot paths: an object per call adds allocation; lambdas help.

Decision gravity. Choose undo-by-inverse when actions are small and reversible; choose snapshots when state is small or inverses are hard. Switching later is a rewrite of every command, so decide early for editors.

Everyday analogy. A pencil with an eraser, plus a notebook of every stroke you made so you can erase them in reverse order.

Common interview traps.

  • Not clearing the redo stack on a new action.
  • Undoing a command whose receiver state has changed since (the stored position is stale).
  • Unbounded history causing OutOfMemoryError.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• State: an object swaps behaviour by delegating to a state object; removes per-method if chains. Kotlin: sealed interface + when for small machines.
  • FSM: states + events + transition table makes illegal moves impossible. Guard transitions atomically in DB (WHERE state='PAID') to avoid double-processing.
  • State vs Strategy: State changes itself via events; Strategy is chosen by the client. Do not use State for two modes or one varying method.
  • Command: a request as an object (Invoker, Command, Receiver) enabling queues, logs, scheduling, retries. Runnable, Handler.post, WorkManager are examples.
  • Undo/redo: two stacks; undo pops and reverses, new action clears redo. Store deltas or inverses, cap the stack, merge keystrokes.
  • Irreversible actions need compensating commands, not undo; persisted commands need stable schemas.
